# forthling

> A Forth-2012 runtime in Rust, for people and AI agents. The core has no dependencies and no `unsafe`; untrusted code runs in a sandbox with a limit on steps (the same result on every machine), time and output, and with files only in memory. It has JSON words, a tutorial, SQLite in memory, an MCP server (`forthling-mcp`) and a playground in the browser (WebAssembly). MIT licence.

This file is for language models that write Forth for forthling, mostly through the MCP server. Everything here was run in forthling.

## Using the MCP server

- `forth_eval` runs code (`code`, and optionally `data`); `forth_stack` shows the stacks; `forth_words` lists the words defined in the session; `forth_reset` starts over.
- The session keeps its definitions, variables and stacks between calls. Define words in one call and use them in the next.
- Each result has the output, the data stack (the top last), the float stack, whether a definition is still open (`compiling`), and the error if there was one: `{"code": -13, "message": "undefined word", "detail": "FOO"}`.
- An error empties the stacks, but the result shows them as they were at the error (`stack`, `fstack`), where it happened (`line`, `column`, `token`) and the words that were running (`words`, such as `MAIN > STEP > /`). An undefined word that is in a word list outside the search order gets a `hint`, such as `ALSO JSON finds it`. Run small pieces, look at the stack, then go on.
- To see what code does word by word, pass `trace: true` to `forth_eval`: the result then has `trace`, each word that ran with its nesting `depth` and the data stack when it started (at most 1000 words; the insides of built-in words are left out). In code, `ALSO DEBUG TRACE-ON … TRACE-OFF` prints the same as output.
- To look at one place, put `BREAK` there (after `ALSO DEBUG`): it does not stop the program, but the result has `breaks`, the stacks and the running words at each `BREAK` (at most 100).
- `steps` and `max_depth` in each result tell how many steps the call took and how deep the data stack went: a depth that grows with each pass of a loop shows a value left behind.
- A line of code, and so a string in `S" "`, is at most 1024 characters. Give larger input, such as a JSON document, as the `data` argument, and read it with `DATA ( -- c-addr u )`, an `ALLOCATE`d copy (`FREE` it). It stays for later calls until another call sends data.
- Files are in memory, never on the disk, at most 4194304 bytes in all, and stay until `forth_reset`. Give source files as the `files` argument of `forth_eval`, `{"square.fs": ": SQUARE DUP * ;"}`, then `INCLUDE square.fs`. The FILE words work on them too: `S" out.txt" W/O CREATE-FILE THROW VALUE OUT  S" hi" OUT WRITE-LINE THROW  OUT CLOSE-FILE THROW`, and a later call can read the file back.
- Each call may take at most 10000000 steps, 5000 ms and 1048576 bytes of output; the session's definitions and the like at most 4194304 bytes in all. A limit reached throws -258 (detail `steps`, `time` or `output`); `CATCH` cannot go on after it.

## Forth in a few lines

- Words are separated by spaces and are not case sensitive. Numbers go on the data stack; words take them off and put results back. `.` prints and drops the top; `.S` shows the stack without changing it.
- `: NAME ... ;` defines a word. `IF ELSE THEN`, `DO LOOP`, `?DO`, `BEGIN UNTIL`, `BEGIN WHILE REPEAT`, `CASE OF ENDOF ENDCASE` work only inside a definition.
- `10 0 DO I . LOOP` counts from 0 to 9: the limit first, then the start. Use `?DO` when the count may be 0.
- Flags: true is -1, false is 0. `1 2 < .` prints -1.
- Strings: `S" text"` gives `( c-addr u )`, and `TYPE` prints it. `." text"` prints, but only inside a definition; outside one use `.( text)`. `S\" a \"quote\"\n"` takes escapes.
- Cells are 64 bits. `123.` (with a dot) is a double-cell number, not a float; a float is `1.5e0` or `3e0`, on the float stack, printed with `F.`.
- `VARIABLE X  5 X !  X @ .` and `5 VALUE N  7 TO N  N .` and `42 CONSTANT ANSWER`.
- Errors: `THROW` with a code, `CATCH` to catch it: `' WORD CATCH` gives 0 or the code. `1 0 /` throws -10.
- Comments: `\ to the end of the line` and `( inside parentheses )`.

## Use locals for more than two or three values

Keeping track of the stack in your head goes wrong easily. Instead of `ROT`, `PICK`, `ROLL` and long chains of `SWAP` and `OVER`, name the inputs:

```forth
: HYP2  {: a b -- c :}  a a *  b b * + ;
3 4 HYP2 .                \ 25
: COUNT-UP  {: n -- :}  n 0 ?DO I . LOOP ;
3 COUNT-UP                \ 0 1 2
```

`{: a b | tmp -- out :}`: the names before `|` take their values from the stack (the last name gets the top), the names after it start at 0, and what follows `--` is only a comment. `x TO a` assigns. Locals work only inside a definition.

## Quotations: nameless words in place

`[: ... ;]` makes a nameless word and leaves its xt, inside a definition or at the prompt. Use it where a word needs an xt and a named definition would be too much.

```forth
: APPLY-TWICE ( x xt -- y )  DUP >R EXECUTE R> EXECUTE ;
3 [: 2 * ;] APPLY-TWICE .        \ 12
```

A quotation does not see the locals of the definition around it; pass values on the stack.

## JSON

`ALSO JSON` makes the JSON words visible. A JSON value is its text, `( c-addr u )`; the reading words give back pieces of it. A missing key or a value of the wrong kind gives the flag 0, not an error.

```forth
ALSO JSON
: DOC  S\" {\"users\": [{\"name\": \"Ada\", \"born\": 1815}]}" ;
DOC S" users[0].born" JSON@ DROP JSON>NUMBER DROP .          \ 1815
DOC S" users[0].name" JSON@ DROP JSON>STRING DROP TYPE       \ Ada (ALLOCATEd)
DOC S" users" JSON@ DROP JSON-LENGTH .                        \ 1
JSON{ S" sum" JSON-KEY 6 JSON-NUMBER S" ok" JSON-KEY -1 JSON-FLAG JSON}
\ prints {"sum":6,"ok":true}
<JSON JSON[ 1 JSON-NUMBER 2 JSON-NUMBER JSON] JSON>          \ ( c-addr u ) [1,2], ALLOCATEd
```

Reading: `JSON-VALID? ( json -- flag )`, `JSON-TYPE ( json -- n )` (0 null, 1 boolean, 2 number, 3 string, 4 array, 5 object, -1 no JSON), `JSON-GET ( json c-addr u -- json' flag )`, `JSON-NTH ( json n -- json' flag )`, `JSON-NAME ( json n -- c-addr u flag )`, `JSON-LENGTH ( json -- n )`, `JSON@ ( json c-addr u -- json' flag )` with a path such as `a.b[2]`, `JSON>NUMBER ( json -- n flag )`, `JSON>FLOAT ( json -- flag ) ( F: -- r )`, `JSON>FLAG ( json -- flag ok )`, `JSON>STRING ( json -- c-addr u flag )`.

Writing goes to the output, or between `<JSON` and `JSON>` to a string; the commas come by themselves: `JSON{ JSON} JSON[ JSON]`, `JSON-KEY ( c-addr u -- )`, `JSON-STRING ( c-addr u -- )`, `JSON-NUMBER ( n -- )`, `JSON-FLOAT ( F: r -- )`, `JSON-FLAG ( flag -- )`, `JSON-NULL`, `JSON-RAW ( json -- )`.

## Tutorial

`ALSO TUTORIAL` gives a Forth course of 20 lessons, ten for beginners and ten beyond, which an agent can walk a person through: `LESSONS` lists them, `n LESSON` shows lesson n (text, code to try, a task), `CHECK` tests the answer the person defined and says what is still wrong, `HINT` gives a hint and `NEXT` the next lesson.

## SQLite

`ALSO SQLITE` gives SQLite words, for databases in memory only: `S" :memory:" DB-OPEN THROW VALUE DB`, then `DB-PREPARE`, `DB-STEP`, `DB-COLUMN` and the like, with errors as an `ior` in the style of the FILE words.

## Regular expressions

`ALSO REGEX` gives regular expressions that match in time linear in the text, so no pattern can hang a program: `RE-MATCH?`, `RE-FIND`, `RE-GROUP`, `RE-COUNT` and `RE-REPLACE`. The text comes first, then the pattern, each as `( c-addr u )`: `S" order 66" S" [0-9]+" RE-FIND` gives `6 2 true` (the start and the length of the match). A bad pattern throws -262.

## HTTP

`ALSO HTTP` gives an HTTP client where the host program allows it: `HTTP-GET ( url-addr url-u -- body-addr body-u status )`, `HTTP-POST ( url-addr url-u body-addr body-u type-addr type-u -- body-addr' body-u' status )`, `HTTP-HEADER` (a header for the next request) and `HTTP-RESPONSE-HEADER`. It is closed by default: it works only for the hosts the program was started with (`--allow-host`), never in the sandbox of `Forth::sandboxed()` or in the playground. The body is ALLOCATEd (FREE it); a status such as 404 is no error; a failed request throws -263, a host that is not allowed -259.
